summary: Describes an extension to the message format to allow character sets other than ASCII in message headers, such as in a name or subject. It was replaced by RFC 1522.

eli5.summary: Email headers could only show basic English letters. This lets names and subjects use other alphabets by writing them in a special coded form that mail programs can turn back.

questions: how do you put non-ascii in email headers
subtitle: Encoding non-ASCII characters in email headers using a printable ASCII wrapper.

tldr.problem: Email headers (like Subject and From) could only contain ASCII characters, preventing users from writing names or subjects in other alphabets like Cyrillic, Greek, or CJK.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1342 defines an 'encoded-word' format that wraps non-ASCII text in a standard ASCII envelope: =?charset?encoding?encoded-text?=. Two encodings are provided: B (Base64) for any text, and Q (Quoted-Printable) for mostly-ASCII text.
tldr.outcome: Email programs can now display names and subjects in any language, even though the underlying message format remains ASCII-only. RFC 1522 later standardized a revised version.

today: RFC 1342 was published as a standards track protocol in June 1992. It was later refined and standardized as RFC 1522, which is the version that became the widely-implemented standard for non-ASCII email headers.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 1341 (MIME) described how to encode the body of an email message in different character sets and to represent that encoded data as printable ASCII. RFC 1342 extends that idea to message headers, which according to RFC 822 are normally limited to ASCII.

The challenge is that many existing email programs have quirks: they delete some headers, rearrange addresses, or reformat header lines. The encoding scheme in RFC 1342 is designed to survive these transformations by using only common printable ASCII characters and by keeping encoded text clearly delimited.
sections.eli5: Email headers (the To, From, and Subject lines) used to only work with English letters. This document provides a way to write them in any language without breaking old email programs that are not careful about following the rules.

sections.title: The Encoded-Word Format
sections.content:
An encoded-word is a special sequence that begins with =?, ends with ?=, and has exactly four question marks in total. The format is:

=?charset?encoding?encoded-text?=

The charset names are defined by RFC 1341; examples include US-ASCII, ISO-8859-1, ISO-8859-2, and others. The encoding field is either B for Base64 or Q for Quoted-Printable. The encoded-text is the actual message, represented using that encoding method.

An encoded-word must be no longer than 75 characters including delimiters. If longer text needs to be encoded, multiple encoded-words may be used, separated by spaces or line breaks. Mail readers that implement this specification recognize the format, decode it, and display the original text in the proper character set.
sections.eli5: The magic format is =?language?method?message?=. The language name says which alphabet to use, the method says how the message is scrambled, and the message is the scrambled text.

sections.title: Encoding Methods
sections.content:
The B encoding (Base64) is identical to the Base64 encoding defined in RFC 1341. It converts any sequence of bytes into a set of 64 safe printable characters. While always safe, it makes the encoded text unreadable to humans; a subject like 'Hello' becomes 'SGVsbG8='.

The Q encoding (Quoted-Printable) is similar to the Quoted-Printable encoding in RFC 1341. Any byte value can be represented as = followed by two hexadecimal digits. For example, =3D is the equals sign, and =20 is a space. Additionally, the underscore character can represent a space, and any byte that corresponds to a printable ASCII character (other than =, ?, or underscore) can be written directly. This makes Q-encoded text with mostly ASCII characters readable at a glance.

Q encoding is recommended for Latin character sets and B encoding for others. However, mail readers must accept either encoding for any character set they support.
sections.eli5: Method B is like a secret code where every character gets replaced. Method Q is like underlining letters that are hard to understand; most of the text stays normal.

sections.title: Use in Message Headers
sections.content:
An encoded-word may appear in specific places in a message header:

In the Subject or Comments field, or any user-defined header field, an encoded-word may replace a word.

Within a comment (text in parentheses), an encoded-word may appear anywhere a comment character would appear. Q-encoded words in comments must not contain the characters (, ), or backslash.

Within a phrase that precedes an address (such as 'John Doe' in 'From: John Doe <john@example.com>'), an encoded-word may replace a word. When used this way, Q-encoded words are restricted to letters, digits, and the characters ! * + - / = _ to ensure the resulting header remains valid.

Importantly, an encoded-word must NOT appear in the actual address portion of a From, To, or Cc field, and must NOT appear in a Received header. These restrictions ensure that old mail handling software will still work correctly.
sections.eli5: You can use the code in subject lines, in names before email addresses, and in comments. But NOT in the email address itself, because that would break old email programs.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content:
Here is a From header with a person's name encoded in ISO-8859-1 (Latin):

From: =?ISO-8859-1?Q?Keld_J=F8rn_Simonsen?= <keld@dkuug.dk>

The =F8 represents the Latin character 'ø' (o with stroke). The underscore replaces a space.

Here is a longer Subject line using Base64 encoding across two encoded-words:

Subject: =?ISO-8859-1?B?SWYgeW91IGNhbiByZWFkIHRoaXMgeW8=?= =?ISO-8859-2?B?dSB1bmRlcnN0YW5kIHRoZSBleGFtcGxlLg==?=

When the mail reader decodes both parts, it reads as 'If you can read this you understand the example.' The second part uses ISO-8859-2 (for Eastern European characters) but in this case only ASCII letters are present.
sections.eli5: In practice, you might write a From header like: From: =?UTF-8?B?4pyTIOOBkuOBhA==?= <person@example.com> for Japanese characters. The email program decodes it back to the original text.
